planting.note: Set divisions into a lean, gritty, neutral-to-alkaline scree or trough mix in full sun; sharp drainage around the crown is essential to prevent rot.

directions: Alpine pink forms a low, dense mat of broad, glossy dark-green leaves that is unusually lush-looking for a high-elevation cushion plant. In early summer it produces relatively large, flat, single flowers in shades of deep pink to rose, each petal finely toothed at the tip, held just above the foliage on short stems. It is native to limestone screes and rocky pastures of the Eastern Alps, where it grows in shallow, stony soil with constant drainage. In the garden it performs best in a raised scree bed or trough with lean, gritty, alkaline soil and prefers cooler summer climates, resenting prolonged heat and humidity around its crown.

planting.note: Plant into a sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; this species is more tolerant of acidic soil than most alpine dianthus but still needs a dry neck.

directions: Maritime Alps pink (long known in cultivation as Dianthus neglectus) forms a tight cushion of narrow, dark-green, almost grass-like leaves that are distinctively buff or fawn-colored on the reverse. Solitary flowers open bright rose-pink to magenta in early summer, each petal notched and curling slightly under so the buff-colored calyx and petal backs show through, a signature trait of the species. It is native to acidic screes and rocky slopes of the Maritime and Cottian Alps, and unlike many alpine pinks it tolerates neutral-to-acidic soils, though it still demands scrupulous drainage. It is an excellent trough and raised-bed subject, flowering most freely where summers stay relatively cool.

planting.note: Sow into a lean, gritty scree mix in full sun; this North American native tolerates dry, rocky soil and resents rich or overly moist ground.

directions: Cutleaf daisy forms a small mound of finely dissected, fern-like gray-green foliage, distinct among rock garden daisies for its lacy leaf texture. From late spring into summer it bears small solitary daisy flowers on short stems, with white, pink-tinged, or occasionally blue rays surrounding a yellow disc, sometimes even lacking rays entirely in some populations. It ranges across gravelly slopes, ridgelines, and talus from the Arctic through the Rocky Mountains, and is one of the most drought- and cold-tolerant daisies suited to a scree bed or gravel garden. It is short-lived but self-sows readily where drainage is sharp and competition from other plants is minimal.

planting.note: Plant divisions into a humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive scree or peat bed in full sun to light shade; unlike most gentians in this genus it prefers steady moisture over drought.

directions: Autumn gentian is a mat-forming, trailing species with narrow, grassy leaves that spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a loose carpet. In early autumn it produces an abundance of large, brilliant deep-blue trumpets, each petal often marked with darker stripes and a paler throat, making it one of the most vividly colored of all autumn-blooming alpines. It is native to alpine meadows and moist stony slopes of the Sino-Himalaya, particularly Yunnan and Sichuan, where it grows in humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil. In cultivation it wants a cooler, damper, more humus-rich position than the classic scree gentians, thriving in a peaty bed or moist trough with acidic soil and protection from hot afternoon sun.

planting.note: Plant into a scrupulously drained tufa crevice or scree mix in full sun with a deep gritty root run; this is among the most difficult alpines in cultivation and largely fails in humid lowland climates.

directions: King of the Alps forms an extremely dense, hard silver cushion of tiny hairy leaves, studded in late spring and early summer with a mass of small, intensely sky-blue flowers with a contrasting white or yellow eye, widely regarded as one of the most beautiful of all cushion alpines. It grows naturally in the highest rocky and gravelly ridges of the European Alps, often above 8,000 feet, where near-constant air movement and a deep, cool, perfectly drained root run keep it dry at the crown year-round. It is notoriously difficult outside true alpine or high-altitude conditions, generally requiring a tufa crevice, deep scree bed, or alpine house with sharp gravel drainage, low summer humidity, and protection from winter wet to persist for more than a season or two.

planting.note: Sow into a lean, sharply drained scree or trough mix in full sun; this Balkan endemic forms a tight mat and needs a dry crown through winter to avoid rot.

directions: Thyme-leaved edraianthus forms a low, spreading mat of tiny, narrow, dark-green leaves reminiscent of a creeping thyme, distinct from its more tightly domed cousins in this genus. In early summer it is covered with upward-facing violet-blue bells held just above the foliage on very short stalks, producing a disproportionately showy display for such a small plant. It is native to limestone rocks and cliffs of the Balkan Peninsula, growing in thin, stony soil with sharp drainage and full exposure. In the rock garden it is best grown in a scree bed, trough, or wall crevice with lean, gritty, alkaline soil, where it spreads gently without becoming invasive and rewards minimal winter wet with reliable flowering.
